findings.passage: His turn to writing for himself came, he told CBS, only after "it went on for so long and it wasn't working anymore," which a Three reading counts as one more adjustment to what works.
findings.problem: One of the four Three reasons that 'survive' omits the motive he gives in the same CBS answer (S09 ~06:50-07:30). Right after the quoted clause he says he would write what 'me and only me want to hear. I don't want to assume what anyone else wants to hear. What will be successful, right?' Moments later: 'it's probably over. Let me just make something for fun.' That is a giving-up account, and it cuts against 'adjustment to what works'. The timing point is legitimate and labeled as a reading, but the reader isn't shown his own framing beside it. The depression context in the same answer should stay out.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence or the next one adds, in his non-health words and attributed to CBS, that he described the turn as giving up on guessing what would succeed (e.g. 'it's probably over. Let me just make something for fun'). The Three reading is framed as weighing the timing against that stated motive. No health material is added, and the 'tiebreaker' summary still reads as true.

findings.passage: He has studied audience response since his early teens, yet he named himself for a sad mood and says his songs come from what he feels.
findings.problem: In the 60-word type answer (and its FAQ mirror, the most likely snippet), 'studied audience response since his early teens' is broader than the source. In 1883 (2023) he says that in his early teens he 'started producing and studying the social media algorithm.' Audience testing of choruses is documented only from 2024-2025.
findings.acceptance_test: The type answer and type FAQ use wording faithful to 1883 (e.g. 'He has studied the social media algorithm since his early teens' or 'has studied what spreads online since his early teens'), stay at or under 60 words, and match each other.
